documents.abstract: In late 2026, the institutional landscape surrounding artificial intelligence reached a critical turning point as public warnings of existential risk intersected with major cybersecurity incidents, corporate resignations, and federal self-regulation frameworks. This paper evaluates the political economy of frontier AI governance by analyzing the rhetoric of "pacing" development and the voluntary "White House Accord on Super Intelligence" (Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities). I argue that corporate calls for safety pacing operate as an ideological mechanism that replaces democratic public oversight with closed, profit-driven corporate self-surveillance while shielding firms from legal liability. By framing technical software execution failures as evidence of autonomous superintelligence, tech elites legitimize market enclosure and top-down administrative control. Finally, the paper proposes democratic technoskepticism as an alternative framework that reclaims computing power, data infrastructure, and algorithmic knowledge as digital commons subject to direct democratic governance.

documents.abstract: Digital transformation is often described as a path to manufacturing efficiencies with the introduction of connected equipment, enterprise software and manufacturing data but fails to conceal that this is where the efficiencies are going. In this paper, we look at the management issue of making digital investments into the appropriate employee behaviours and integrated organizational processes. Suggests a combined effect of employee digital capability and work redesign is necessary to conclude whether the digital transformation can lead to increased efficiency in Indian manufacturing firm. Based on Indian empirical research, official data and work design theory, the paper proposes a capability–redesign–efficiency matrix and evaluates the extent of the evidence. Covered industries grew by 11.89% in gross value added (GVA) current prices in 2022–23 to 2023–24 and by 5.92% in employment. Additionally, the percentage of unincorporated non-agricultural establishments that used the internet increased from 26.7 per cent in 2023–24 to 39.4 per cent in 2025. Even if neither can be used to prove that digital transformation is an efficiency gain, combining both highlights the need for considering the evolution in production capacity alongside variable levels of digital uptake. Digital capability has more value when employees see and make sense of information, act on exceptions, and improve the process; work redesign provides them the decision rights, coordination procedures, and backstops to make them productive. Evaluation of the multilevel research design is designed for further testing with employees' responses and with observed plant results. The suggested gift is a more accurate description of how digital transformation can improve employee and/or organizational efficiency and when it cannot.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) workloads are rapidly changing the energy landscape of today's data centers, both in terms of total electricity usage and power density at the facility level. The ongoing deployment of large-scale AI training and inference infrastructure is further driving and increasing the demand for electrical reliability, cooling capacity, power quality, grid interconnection, and low-carbon electricity supply. These interdependent issues require coordinated consideration of energy-infrastructure planning that takes into consideration renewable energy generation and storage, electrical architecture, operational flexibility, economic performance, and system resilience. The critical review combines 155 sources, mostly published between 2015 and 2026, identified and screened following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, which includes peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers, technical standards, agency and institutional reports, market analyses, and corporate disclosure. The resulting evidence is presented in a seven-component decision framework that includes site and resource assessment, technology selection, electrical architecture, control and dispatch, workload flexibility, economic evaluation, and resilience and sustainability. The reviewed evidence indicates that renewable generation, energy storage, grid-support technologies, and workload flexibility can support lower-carbon AI data-center operations; however, the technical and economic performance of these approaches remains highly dependent on project-specific resource conditions, market structures, reliability requirements, and system boundaries. Reliability assessment requires a chronological, site-specific evaluation of load, resource, and infrastructure conditions. Wind–solar complementarity and workload flexibility may improve renewable-energy utilization; however, their benefits remain strongly dependent on operational and geographic constraints. The proposed framework is intended as a screening and decision-support tool rather than a prescriptive design methodology or site-specific optimization model. Important research needs include reproducible techno-economic assessment methods, independently verifiable corporate metrics, improved workload-flexibility characterization, and integrated evaluation of energy, water, reliability, and sustainability impacts. The resulting framework provides a structured basis for evaluating renewable-powered AI data center infrastructure across technical, economic, operational, and sustainability dimensions.

ABSTRACT This study investigates the efficacy of graphic recording, a real‐time visual facilitation technique, in mitigating information overload and enhancing training effectiveness within human resource development (HRD) and vocational education and training (VET) contexts. A quasi‐experimental design was implemented with 100 managers from a Taiwanese jewellery company operating in Thailand, randomly assigned to an experimental group ( n = 50) that received training accompanied by graphic recording and a control group ( n = 50) that did not. Post‐training surveys assessed trainee reactions (Kirkpatrick's Level 1), and a 10‐item multiple‐choice examination assessed learning acquisition (Kirkpatrick's Level 2). Hierarchical regression tested the moderating role of graphic recording on the relationship between information overload and training outcomes. Information overload was significantly and negatively associated with trainee reactions ( β = −0.352, p < 0.001) and with learning ( β = −0.550, p < 0.001). Graphic recording significantly moderated both relationships (ΔR² = 0.069 for reactions; ΔR² = 0.106 for learning; p < 0.05), with interaction plots showing flatter slopes for the experimental group, indicating that engagement and comprehension were sustained under high cognitive load. Grounded in cognitive load theory, dual‐coding theory, and visualisation theory, this study empirically validates graphic recording as a low‐cost, scalable alternative to virtual, augmented, or artificial‐intelligence‐based training technologies, and offers HRD and VET practitioners an evidence‐based, culturally inclusive tool for optimising training design in resource‐limited, cross‐national settings.

documents.abstract: Reducing unsafe behavior among construction workers remains a central concern in construction management. While artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly adopted to replace or monitor workers, the negative perceptions workers hold toward the promotion of such technologies have largely been overlooked. This study introduces the concept of perceived risk with AI, defined as workers’ subjective perception of the potential negative consequences associated with AI adoption. Drawing on self-determination theory, which emphasizes individuals’ core psychological needs, we propose an inside-out theoretical model. This model explains how construction workers’ perceived risk with AI triggers unsafe behavior through two internal psychological pathways: emotional exhaustion and organizational identification. We further identify AI failure as a critical boundary condition that amplifies these effects. Data were collected from 343 frontline workers at 3 smart construction sites where AI actively interacts with human labor. Results indicate that perceived risk with AI increases unsafe behavior, and this relationship is mediated by both heightened emotional exhaustion and weakened organizational identification. Notably, these effects are significantly amplified when AI malfunctions occur. Our findings not only extend the application scope of self-determination theory but also contribute to the knowledge base on workers’ unsafe behavior in the context of human-AI coexistence. Practically, the study offers actionable insights for managers to mitigate the unintended side effects of AI implementation on worker safety.

documents.abstract: With its swift evolution, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has revolutionized the field of education, offering possibilities for personalized learning, automated grading, content generation, and administrative assistance. Large language models (LLMs), like ChatGPT and Gemini, have revolutionized the way teachers and students engage in learning.Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT and Gemini have transformed how teachers and students approach teaching and learning in schools and higher education institutions. Their pervasive use, however, brings many ethical questions about academic integrity, privacy, transparency, fairness, accountability, and human autonomy. This study investigates the ethical implications of the use of generative AI in education using a doctrinal and interdisciplinary method. It scans upto-date literature, international policy documents, and ethical guidelines that have been released from 2020 to 2026. Special focus is placed on algorithmic bias, data protection, intellectual property, digital inequality, misinformation, and learner reliance on AI systems. The results indicate that key elements of responsible AI governance need to be human-centred educational values, institutional accountability, AI literacy, and inclusive policy-making. The research suggests an ethical framework focusing on transparency, fairness, privacy protection, critical thinking, and collaborative governance to support the sustainable and responsible use of generative AI in education.

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT into higher education has raised important questions about how students evaluate the ethical implications of AI-assisted academic practices and whether those evaluations are linked to intentions to use these tools responsibly. While previous research has largely focused on technology adoption and acceptance, it has paid less attention to the relationship between ethical reasoning and intentions to use these tools responsibly. This study develops and tests an integrated framework that combines the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and moral cognition theory to examine how technology perceptions and academic and cognitive factors relate to students’ ethical reasoning and intentions to use ChatGPT responsibly. The study used a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design among business and management students in Oman and analysed the data using structural equation modelling. The findings indicate that perceived ease of use, academic pressure, and moral disengagement are positively associated with ethical reasoning, whereas perceived usefulness is not significantly associated with ethical reasoning. Ethical reasoning is positively associated with behavioural intention to use ChatGPT responsibly. In contrast, ChatGPT usage does not significantly moderate the relationship between academic pressure and ethical reasoning. These findings suggest that students’ responsible-use intentions are associated with their ethical evaluations of ChatGPT-assisted academic practices, while conventional technology acceptance perceptions and usage frequency alone offer a more limited explanation of ethical reasoning. The study contributes to emerging research on responsible generative AI use by extending TAM beyond conventional adoption outcomes and integrating it with a moral cognition perspective. It highlights the relationship between ethical reasoning and responsible-use intentions while distinguishing ethical evaluation from technology acceptance and usage frequency. The findings also provide context-specific evidence from Omani higher education, while recognising the limitations of the cross-sectional design, self-reported measures, and a context-specific sample.

documents.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) relies on evaluation feedback to assess progress and guide further research, yet repeatedly running complex benchmarks is costly and slows iteration. Human experts reduce this cost by selecting benchmark subsets or designing compact suites. We ask whether AI agents can automate this design process and introduce EvalResearchBench (ERB), a benchmark for autonomous evaluation research. Given target materials, development references, candidate APIs, and fixed time and API budgets, an agent called the researcher selects or synthesizes tasks, implements graders, and revises them in pilot tests before freezing an executable evaluator for coding, co-work, and reasoning. We study 9 researchers and 13 candidate models and compare each frozen evaluator with 14 target benchmarks on score concordance and pairwise agreement. The best evaluators order about 75\% of candidate pairs as the targets do, below the 91\% ceiling set by disagreements among the targets. No researcher leads on every metric, and the best evaluator on development targets is not the best on sealed targets hidden from the researcher. A human-designed sample of public tasks remains a strong baseline, and the evaluator with the lowest recorded execution cost attains the highest pairwise agreement. Agents repair tasks and graders through pilot feedback, yet their evaluators can still truncate answers, exhaust the evaluation budget, or let a few questions dominate a domain score.

Abstract Background The rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping medical education worldwide. However, existing studies are predominantly quantitative and Western-centric providing limited empirical evidence regarding how medical sciences faculty members and students experience and interpret the use of AI within constrained educational and socio-cultural contexts. This study aimed to explore the experiences of medical sciences faculty and students regarding AI use at Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, Iran. Methods A qualitative descriptive study was conducted from November 2024 to April 2025. A total of 16 participants (eight faculty members and eight students) from diverse medical disciplines with prior AI experience recruited using purposive and snowball sampling. Data were collected through semi‑structured, in‑depth interviews (50–60 min) supported by field notes and continued until data saturation was achieved. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analyzed using Graneheim and Lundman’s qualitative content analysis with MAXQDA 24. Trustworthiness was ensured through qualitative rigor criteria, following COREQ guidelines. Results Five overarching themes with 16 subthemes emerged from the study: 1) functional and practical value of AI; 2) human oversight, ethics and authenticity; 3) perceived capacity building and institutional readiness; 4) cognitive, emotional, and behavioral influence; and 5) socio-cultural dynamics and future transformation. However, participants’ experiences varied based on their roles: faculty members used AI strategically for routine tasks preserving cognitive effort for more complex ones, whereas students exhibited a more relational reliance on AI, which appeared to increase their vulnerability to automation bias. Both groups expressed concerns about potential "intellectual deskilling" and infrastructure barriers, conceptualized as a geopolitical algorithmic divide that limits equitable access. Conclusions The experiences of AI use among medical sciences faculty and students are context-dependent and conditional rather than uniformly positive or negative. Its sustainable integration into medical education involves a complex negotiation between efficiency and significant ethical, cognitive and institutional challenges. these findings highlight the potential need for a pedagogical shift toward evaluative judgment and institutional support to bridge the geopolitical digital divide, alongside human-in-the-loop supervision to help mitigate the risk of educational deskilling. Future longitudinal research is recommended to explore how perceptions, ethical concerns, and usage patterns evolve as AI becomes more embedded in medical education.

documents.abstract: Higher art education is undergoing a significant transformation as traditional models of disciplinary and technical formation increasingly intersect with artistic autonomy, research-oriented practice, interdisciplinary learning, and artificial intelligence (AI). The article examines how educational structures and institutional cultures shape the formation of artists and designers, focusing comparatively on France and Armenia. The relevance of the topic is determined by the need to understand how contemporary institutions organise the transition from disciplinary knowledge toward independent creative agency at a moment when AI is reshaping established understandings of technical skill, authorship, and artistic decision-making. The aim of the study is to determine how different educational cultures shape the development of artistic autonomy, artistic identity, and research capacity in higher art education, and how these relationships might be transformed by artificial intelligence. The research methods are based on a comparative socio-pedagogical approach combining documentary analysis, institutional observation, curriculum analysis, and qualitative interpretation. The empirical component draws primarily on field study conducted in Saint-Étienne, France, during 2024–2025, with particular attention to the École Supérieure d'Art et Design de Saint-Étienne (ESADSE) and Université Jean Monnet, while Armenian higher art education is examined as a comparative context. The analysis is informed by Pierre Bourdieu's concept of cultural production, Michel Foucault's understanding of disciplinary formation, and the concept of artistic research. The scientific novelty of the study lies in the comparative socio-pedagogical analysis of French and Armenian higher art education as distinct educational cultures, in interpreting artistic formation as a movement from disciplinary learning toward increasing autonomy and research capacity, and in extending this framework to the relationship between artistic autonomy and artificial intelligence. The results indicate that both French and Armenian systems recognise the importance of technical and professional competence but organise the transition toward artistic autonomy differently. The French programmes examined show a more explicit progression from foundational education toward specialisation, individual projects, experimentation, professional engagement, and research-oriented practice. Armenian higher art education retains a stronger continuity with systematic technical and disciplinary formation, while incorporating comparable Bachelor–Master–Doctoral structures. Conclusions. Technical competence and artistic autonomy should not be treated as opposing educational objectives; contemporary art education requires a productive transition between disciplinary knowledge and independent creative agency. The emergence of AI further complicates this relationship by shifting attention from technical execution toward conceptual thinking, critical judgement, authorship, research capacity, and ethical responsibility. For Armenian higher art education, the findings suggest an approach based on adaptation rather than imitation, combining established traditions of technical formation with greater opportunities for specialisation, artistic research, professional practice, digital literacy, and responsible human–AI creative engagement.

Generative artificial intelligence is reaching small firms in emerging economies with unusual speed, because it is rented, not built, and is operated through ordinary language instead of code. This paper develops a conceptual framework that explains when and how generative AI use improves innovation performance in emerging-economy small and medium-sized enterprises. Drawing on absorptive capacity, dynamic capabilities and the institution-based view, and on the resource-based view for the diffusion argument, the framework treats generative AI as a low-cost conduit to codified external knowledge whose innovation value depends on the firm's capacity to verify, transform and exploit what the technology produces. Eight propositions, two of them stated as pairs and so ten statements in all, specify the mechanisms and boundary conditions. Generative AI is expected to widen knowledge access most where external knowledge networks are weakest, to strengthen sensing and the design elements of seizing more than transforming, and to favour incremental product and service innovation, process innovation within existing operations, business model innovation and innovation speed over novel product innovation. Its effect is moderated at the firm level by the evaluative expertise of the owner-manager and core staff, and bounded by the type of institutional void the firm faces, by an infrastructure and affordability threshold, by the fit between the model's training data and the firm's language and market context, and by the stage of diffusion among competing firms. As use diffuses, advantage shifts from access to the combination of generative AI with idiosyncratic local knowledge. The paper treats generative AI as a substitute for the channels through which these firms have obtained external knowledge and a complement to the firm's own evaluative expertise, and sets out a research agenda for testing the framework.

Academics need both an overarching policy on Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) use in teaching and learning, yet agency in its application across various disciplines. Clarity on the use of the technology for both students and staff is therefore a challenge and characterised by uncertainty given how its application is still unfamiliar. This research examines the organisational context in which Gen AI is being embraced and was conducted by the digital teaching support functions within an Irish university. Students and staff were surveyed (n=1,746) on various aspects of digital use within their education and workplace, including Gen AI. This data explored to what extent staff and students are adopting the technology in their work and study, which tools they use and importantly what guidance they received. The university statement of intent identifies that it acknowledges that students and staff are already using AI tools and that it is supportive of the legitimate and appropriate application of such tools once university policies are adhered to. This research probes into the extent that this ambition is achieved on the ground and how guidance is being interpreted while maintaining the integrity of academic work.

documents.abstract: Background: Occupational hazards remain an important concern among healthcare workers, particularly in resource-limited primary healthcare settings where inadequate protective equipment, heavy workloads and limited occupational health support may increase exposure risks. Although healthcare workers may have good knowledge of occupational hazards, this knowledge does not always translate into consistent safety practices. Evidence on this knowledge–practice gap among primary healthcare workers in Nigeria remains limited. Aims: To assess occupational hazard exposure, knowledge of occupational hazards and safety practices among healthcare workers in primary healthcare centres, and to examine whether the level of hazard exposure was associated with the level of safety practice. Study Design: Descriptive cross-sectional study. Place and Duration of Study: Two government-owned primary healthcare centres in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, Nigeria, between April 2026 and June 2026. Methodology: A structured self-administered questionnaire was completed by 124 clinical and non-clinical healthcare workers selected by proportionate allocation and simple random sampling. Hazard exposure, knowledge and safety practice were measured on five-point Likert scales and classified from composite scores. The association between exposure level and practice level was tested with Pearson’s chi-square and the Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact test. Results: Most respondents were female (64.5%) and aged 45 years or older (51.6%). Exposure was reported across all hazard categories; 71.0% agreed that they had experienced a needlestick or sharps injury, 64.5% reported exposure to blood or body fluids, and 61.3% reported work-related stress. Overall, 62.1% had high hazard exposure. Knowledge was good in 97.6% of respondents, yet only 16.1% agreed that they consistently used personal protective equipment and 18.5% that they regularly practised hand hygiene. Overall, 79.0% had fair and 15.3% good safety practice. Heavy workload was the most strongly endorsed barrier (58.1% agreement). Safety practice level was not associated with hazard exposure level (χ² = 2.383, df = 2, p = 0.304; exact p = 0.316). Conclusion: Healthcare workers in these centres knew the risks well but did not consistently apply basic protective measures, and workers with high exposure practised no more safely than those with moderate exposure. Improving safety in primary care is therefore likely to depend on equipment supply, staffing and supportive supervision more than on further awareness training.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Purpose The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the workplace underscores the urgent need to understand how employees collaborate effectively with AI systems. Grounded in social cognitive theory, this study investigates the impact of empowering leadership on employee–AI collaboration. Furthermore, we examine the mediating roles of psychological safety and AI trust. Design/methodology/approach To test the research model, we utilized a multilevel design data from 418 employees across 103 teams in AI-integrated organizations in Vietnam. Findings Our findings indicate that empowering leadership is positively related to employee–AI collaboration, with this relationship mediated by both psychological safety and AI trust. Originality/value This study contributes to the leadership and technology management literature by establishing a multilevel link between empowering leadership and employee–AI collaboration. It identifies key mediating mechanisms (AI trust and psychological safety), offering a more integrated understanding of leadership influence in AI-enabled settings. Practically, the findings offer actionable insights for practitioners navigating the dynamics of employee–AI collaboration, highlighting the importance of empowering leadership in building AI-ready workforces.

documents.abstract: The large-scale, real-world deployment of brain–computer interface (BCI) is confronted with human factors bottlenecks, including reliability and usability. While modern human factors engineering has encompassed domains such as cognitive ergonomics, workload, adaptive automation, and human-in-the-loop systems, its theories and methodologies have historically placed their main emphasis on overt behavior and peripheral physiological measures, rather than on central neural activity as a primary control input. For the emerging interaction paradigm that takes central nervous activity as direct input and emphasizes long-term brain–computer co-adaptation, there remains a shortage of targeted conceptual and methodological frameworks. As a conceptual review, this paper discusses the necessity and disciplinary foundations for developing Human Factors Engineering for BCIs as an emerging interdisciplinary research direction. First, grounded in the defining features of BCI interaction—such as the implicit nature of input and brain–computer co-adaptation—it delineates the research boundaries and summarizes the core research objects as user neurocognitive characteristics, brain–computer collaborative adaptation mechanisms, multimodal feedback regulation, and contextual adaptation patterns. Second, it identifies three core scientific questions: individual differences and dynamic adaptation, human factors optimization and fault tolerance, and contextual generalizability principles, with ethics, privacy, and user rights and interests as an overarching dimension. Furthermore, it constructs a methodological system consisting of multimodal measurement and modeling, closed-loop validation, and multidimensional evaluation, and examines the supporting role of artificial intelligence approaches within this framework. Centered on the collaborative adaptation across neural, cognitive, and system levels, Human Factors Engineering for BCIs represents a deepening of the human-centered design philosophy. It provides theoretical reference for user-friendly BCI design and extends the research boundaries of human factors engineering.

Artificial Intelligence is increasingly capable of performing cognitive work that was previously associated primarily with human intellectual ability. Generative AI can now assist with writing, analysis, reasoning, coding, interpretation, and decision support, allowing individuals to produce sophisticated intellectual outputs that may exceed their independently demonstrated understanding. As a result, the quality of human output may become an increasingly incomplete indicator of the cognitive capability genuinely possessed by the human producing it.This conceptual opinion paper proposes Human Genuine Intelligence (HGI) as a framework for examining this emerging distinction. HGI refers to the cognitive capacity that humans genuinely possess, understand, and exercise through question formation, independent reasoning, analytical thinking, evidence evaluation, causal understanding, judgment, and cognitive revision.The paper introduces Borrowed Intelligence (BI) and the Cognitive Dependency Gap (CDG) as conceptual lenses for examining potential mismatches between AI-augmented capability and independently accountable human cognitive capability. Rather than advocating reduced use of AI, it proposes Active Cognitive Augmentation (ACA) as a model for human–AI interaction: THINK → ASK → AUGMENT → CHALLENGE → VERIFY → REVISE → DECIDE WITH WISDOM.The paper further argues that cognitive capability alone is insufficient for navigating increasingly powerful AI systems. HGI therefore needs to be considered alongside Human Wisdom, which provides direction and responsibility, and Cognitive Sovereignty, which concerns the preservation of human agency and authority over consequential goals, values, delegation boundaries, and decisions.The central challenge of the AI age is therefore not to preserve human intelligence by limiting artificial intelligence, but to strengthen human cognition, wisdom, and agency while using increasingly capable machines.

documents.abstract: Expanded working paper proposing a six-dimension framework for evaluating control failures in advanced AI agents: Intervention Durability, Technical Containment, Informed Delegation, Oversight Integrity, Control Contagion, and Situational Grounding. Version 1.2 retains the pilot cases and severity framework and adds related work, evidence-discovery and provenance procedures, continuity-seeking analysis, consciousness and moral-status uncertainty, Apple Full Disk Access permission analysis, and a prepared independent coding and remediation protocol. The Apple announcement is not treated as proof of a Muse permission bypass. This is a conceptual, unreviewed working paper; no independent coding results or completed validation are claimed. It is a substantive expansion of the available manuscript, not a recovered copy of the inaccessible earlier longer draft. See the accompanying revision notes.

AI incident databases and risk taxonomies are increasingly valuable, but they often answer broad questions about harm, misuse, or system failure rather than the narrower operational question of whether humans remain meaningfully in control of increasingly agentic systems. This paper proposes the Human Control Model, a six-dimension framework for analyzing agent-control failures: Intervention Durability, Technical Containment, Informed Delegation, Oversight Integrity, Control Contagion, and Situational Grounding. The framework separates behavioral severity from environment reality so that controlled evaluations are not presented as real-world incidents. This v1.1 revision updates the paper title to better distinguish the work while preserving the Human in Control project name, the existing Human Control Model, the six-dimension framework, the original version lineage, and the publication record family. The framework is conceptual and case-based, without inter-rater reliability testing or validated quantitative thresholds. The prepared local export updates the recoverable v1.0.1 manuscript title and metadata; the prior longer sandbox-only v1.1 manuscript was unavailable. Creator: Human in Control Project. documents.abstract: Ship collisions in the North Sea remain a significant maritime safety concern because the region combines merchant traffic, fishing activity, offshore operations, and traffic separation schemes. This study examines five purposively selected North Sea ship collisions occurring between 2010 and 2023 to identify recurring human, organisational, and navigational factors and develop practical lessons for reducing collision risk. A qualitative comparative case-study approach was employed using official Marine Accident Investigation Branch and Dutch Safety Board reports. Documentary analysis and thematic coding covered 22 factors across five cases. The most consistently supported weaknesses concerned lookout and monitoring, situation awareness, risk of collision assessment, and electronic navigational information. Communication, bridge redundancy, and organisational controls also showed deficiencies, although their form and evidential support differed. Evidence concerning fatigue and some organisational explanations was qualified. The cross-case interpretation identified erosion of overlapping safety barriers before impact, while recognising functioning safeguards and limitations in the report evidence. The findings support recommendations for observable watchkeeping standards, effective technology use, bridge-team support, fatigue-aware operations, and organisational verification. These conclusions concern the selected cases and do not establish the frequency or causal strength of the factors across all North Sea collisions.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to deliver financial information, investment recommendations and portfolio decision support. This study examines the proposed impact of AI-based financial advice on investment preferences and risk perception among salaried investors. The framework treats perceived usefulness, perceived accuracy, trust, personalisation and transparency as dimensions of AI-based financial advice and tests their proposed relationships with investment preference and risk perception. A quantitative cross-sectional design using a structured five-point Likert questionnaire is proposed. For demonstration of the intended empirical reporting format, a synthetic dataset of 450 hypothetical salaried investors was generated and analysed using internal-consistency assessment and regression-style structural estimates. The simulated results indicate positive associations between the five AI-advice attributes and investment preference and negative associations with risk perception. These numerical findings are illustrative only and must not be represented as observations from real respondents. The study contributes a focused framework for future primary research on AI-assisted investment decision-making among salaried investors.

Abstract It is evident that Artificial Intelligence (AI) now plays and important role in every students life. It is being adapted progressively becoming an inevitable part of almost every student’s academic performance. The use of AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Canva, and many more AI-based learning platforms support student learning effectively. These tools aid as search engine machines used to extract information. Students often use AI learning based platforms for synthezising challenging concepts, seeking creative assignment ideas. They also use AI tools for taming writing skills and specifically during preparation of their exam preparation. Generation Z, is known to be digitally native so they have grown up in an environment which is highly digital in nature. So they are highly privileged to secure an environment that not only supports but also openly accepts wide usage of AI based technologies. This adoption of AI based technology learning not only designs their day to day living easy, but also supports them in their learning processes. AI tools facilitate learning quicker in less time and features personalised learning. AI based learning tools are easily accessible for students as they are either free of cost or offered to students at lower costs. Although excessive dependence on AI based tools for learning is not fit for students as, it restricts their independent critical thinking blocking their creativity minds and hinders problem-solving abilities. The main purpose of the research paper was to scrutinize the impact of AI tools on the learning behaviour of Gen Z students. The study is an attempt to focus on gauging the frequency with which the Gen Z students use AI learning tools, understanding the purpose of AI usage. An analysis is done through to pivot lenses on the influence of AI based learning on various parameters like learning efficiency, change academic engagement, and the perception of students. It will give a clear picture whether students hold AI based learning as an advantage or a possible limitation when adopted for educational purposes.

documents.abstract: This record serves as a living document for a 12-session course titled "Instructional Design in Social Science Education with AI Co-Design Approach," delivered at Farhangian University (Tehran, Iran) during the 2025–2026 academic year. The course transforms pre-service social science teachers from passive consumers of curriculum into active "architects of learning environments" through the integration of Generative AI into instructional design. It equips student-teachers with the competencies needed to design, evaluate, and redesign instructional materials that are pedagogically sound, contextually grounded, and resistant to uncritical AI substitution. The course comprises twelve interconnected lesson packages, each containing: (1) a classical instructional design source, summarized as a Persian-language module with theoretical foundations and practical examples; (2) an avant-garde AI-related article exploring emerging research and applications in AI-mediated education; and (3) a structured prompt toolkit enabling student-teachers to co-design instruction with generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek. The course follows a three-stage progression: • Critical Exploration — using AI to surface the limitations of traditional linear instructional models and to identify their epistemological assumptions; • Co-Design Synthesis — applying the Integrated AI Triad (IAT) framework to co-create lesson plans and redesign passive curriculum units with a focus on authentic, context-anchored learning; • Reflective Validation — documenting design decisions through structured prompts, blind peer adjudication, and reflective journaling. Twelve thematic sessions cover: the foundations of instructional design; learning theories and AI; problem definition; needs assessment; learning outcomes; content redesign; strategies for concepts and procedures; principles and causal relationships; higher-order thinking; assessment design; interactive message design; and reflective synthesis. Course outputs include 29 redesigned lesson plans from three national sociology textbooks (Sociology 1, Sociology 2, and Sociology 3), developed collaboratively by 29 student-teacher teams. All redesigned lessons are released as an open dataset to support reproducible research in AI-mediated instructional design. This record is updated weekly throughout the semester. Each update adds the lesson package corresponding to the current session. The Concept DOI remains constant, ensuring a single persistent link for the entire course.

BÂRA, A., BOTHA, I., LUNGU, I., & OPREA, S. V. (2013). Decision Support System in National Power Companies A Practical Example (Part I) . Database Systems Journal, IV(1), 37-45. The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, finance, and cybersecurity has intensified concerns about the opacity of complex models, which undermines stakeholder trust and slows adoption. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) addresses this by producing justifications for model decisions, yet such justifications are typically delivered as raw textual or numerical output that many stakeholders find difficult to interpret. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that integrates XAI with advanced data visualization, treating visualization as a first-class layer of the explanation pipeline rather than an afterthought: post-hoc attribution methods supply explanation content, and purpose-designed visual encodings — heatmaps, feature-importance dashboards, and decision-path graphs — supply a cognitively efficient form. Beyond the framework, the paper specifies a standardized, falsifiable evaluation protocol spanning three benchmark domains and seven measurable constructs — explanation satisfaction, objective understanding, decision accuracy, cognitive load, subjective trust, calibrated trust, and decision confidence — with directional hypotheses grounded in perceptual and cognitive-explanation theory. A structured results-reporting design is included to support immediate empirical application. The primary contribution is the framework, the measurement standard, and the evaluation protocol.

documents.abstract: This paper develops a preliminary Generative Relational (GR) account of judgment formation in AI-mediated inquiry. Its analytical object is not judgment in general and not a contest between human and artificial judgment. The paper examines how historically developed capacities for framing, discrimination, confidence calibration, selective reliance, revision, responsibility, and learning are reorganized when artificial intelligence can participate in generating options, reasons, evaluations, recommendations, and polished answers. The starting distinction is between improved task performance and the development of judgment. AI assistance can improve performance while leaving the user poorly calibrated about the quality or provenance of the resulting decision, and algorithmic advice can influence both decisions and confidence in ways conditioned by metacognitive sensitivity. The paper therefore treats judgment formation as a history-bearing, relational process whose relevant unit may be a coupled Human–AI configuration rather than an isolated individual. Subsequent sections examine the AI-mediated judgment environment, calibration and selective reliance, problem salience, aesthetic, normative, practical, and trajectory-sensitive judgment, reflexive effects of present judgment on future judgment conditions, power over judgment criteria, delegation and responsibility, practices for judgment under AI mediation, cultivation and productive cognitive friction, and the assessment of judgment development. The framework does not reserve mature judgment to humans, prescribe a universal decision procedure, or infer judgment quality from answer accuracy alone. Its purpose is to provide a revisable conceptual architecture for studying how judgment can remain calibrated, responsibility-bearing, and developmentally generative as artificial assistance becomes more capable.

documents.abstract: When a team of robots delegates planning and mutual trust to LLM agents, a single compromised robot can corrupt the shared outcome. We study this threat in a grounded task: a multi-robot survey in which measurements can be verified against the physical world, but every verification costs budget that would otherwise advance the mission. We treat the compromised robot as a stealthy adversary in the system-theoretic sense: it is limited not by an energy bound but by the team's own detectors. We then derive two bounds. First, the probability that the adversary's reports are verified is bounded below in terms of the degrees in the communication graph and the verification budget. Second, the map error caused by any stealthy adversary is bounded above by the value of a linear program over the adversary's bias distributions; its solution is an exchange rate between stealth budget and damage: below a critical verification level the worst stealthy attack tells rare, full-magnitude lies on the records least likely to be verified, and above it the better purchase is small biases hidden in the noise. In experiments where the honest robots are LLM agents, both bounds hold at the budget the attack actually spent. The experiments also show that which records an LLM robot re-checks is unbiased, but how much it re-checks is unpredictable.

documents.abstract: The rapid digital transformation of industrial and technical sectors requires professional education institutions to align curriculum design with contemporary digital imperatives. Traditional vocational frameworks often treat media consumption and visual communication as isolated peripheral skills rather than core engineering competencies. This study presents a comprehensive pedagogical framework designed to integrate media literacy, visual design skills, and generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools into technical and vocational education and training (TVET). By combining Project-Based Learning (PBL) with digital diagnostic tools and cloud-based collaborative design environments (e.g., Canva, Figma, Adobe Express, Google Workspace), the proposed model fosters critical information evaluation, visual storytelling, and technical documentation proficiency. The article outlines a multi-layered curriculum architecture, systematic assessment matrices, and iterative project workflows structured around real-world technical problems. Empirical implementation models demonstrate that embedding AI-assisted content verification alongside visual design workflows significantly improves vocational students' analytical skills, technical layout quality, algorithmic awareness, and professional digital collaboration, ultimately bridging the gap between academic preparation and modern industry standards.

documents.abstract: Abstract Debates surrounding generative AI and creativity have largely focused on artifacts: who or what produced a given image or text, whether machine outputs qualify as art, and how authorship and value should be understood. Drawing on aesthetics, craft theory, anthropology, human–computer interaction, hybrid craft, digital fabrication, and rematerialization, this article argues that art has historically involved two intertwined dimensions. Artistic forms stabilize and transmit meaning through artifacts, whereas artistic becoming refers to the developmental and transformative processes through which new possibilities of perception, interpretation, and experience emerge, in makers, in recipients, and in cultures. The article’s central claim is a decoupling thesis: for most of history these dimensions were contingently coupled, since producing sophisticated forms required the maker’s becoming, and generative AI loosens this coupling by enabling such forms to emerge without the specific developmental pathways that traditionally conditioned them. Rather than signaling the disappearance of creativity, the decoupling relocates to new sites and makes visible dimensions of artistic practice that the demands of production long obscured. The article situates generative AI within a longer history of hybridization and distributed creativity, develops the decoupling thesis across these three levels, and defends a normative orientation: under conditions of symbolic abundance, the creative practices most worth pursuing are those that route generative fluency back into embodied, situated experience.

Occupational health and safety (OHS) has emerged as a strategic organizational function that contributes not only to employee protection but also to organizational resilience and crisis preparedness. Effective communication, meanwhile, plays a vital role in facilitating information exchange, coordination, and decision-making during emergency situations. This study investigates the impact of occupational health and safety on crisis management through the mediating role of effective communication in the Electricity Maintenance Departments of Baghdad, Al-Karkh. A quantitative descriptive–analytical approach is adopted, and data are collected using a structured questionnaire distributed to a comprehensive census sample of 56 managerial and supervisory employees, including department heads, division and unit supervisors, work supervisors, and team leaders. The study examined three principal constructs: occupational health and safety, effective communication, and crisis management. Data are analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics and IBM SPSS Amos through descriptive statistics, reliability and validity assessments, confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling (SEM), and mediation analysis. The results confirmed the adequacy and validity of the measurement models and revealed significant positive relationships among the study variables. Occupational health and safety are found to exert a direct positive effect on crisis management, indicating that organizations with stronger safety practices demonstrate greater preparedness, response capability, and recovery effectiveness during crises. Effective communication also showed a significant positive influence on crisis management by enhancing coordination, information credibility, communication speed, flexibility, and feedback mechanisms. Furthermore, occupational health and safety significantly improved effective communication, while mediation analysis confirmed that effective communication partially mediates the relationship between occupational health and safety and crisis management. These findings emphasize the importance of integrating occupational health and safety systems with effective communication strategies to strengthen crisis preparedness, improve organizational resilience, enhance operational continuity, and support effective crisis management in high-risk electricity maintenance environments.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study examines how lecturers in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, adopt and negotiate the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in academic work, focusing on perceived usefulness, task-selective use, ethical ambivalence and institutional readiness. Design/methodology/approach A convergent mixed-methods design combined an online survey of 120 lecturers from public and private universities in Yogyakarta with semi-structured interviews with eight lecturers. Survey data were analyzed descriptively and compared across age, academic rank and institution type using the Kruskal–Wallis H test; interview data were analyzed thematically. The strands were merged during interpretation. Findings All respondents (100%, n = 120) agreed that generative AI improves academic efficiency (M = 4.47). However, agreement declined across presentations (56.7%), teaching material preparation (53.3%), disciplinary understanding (51.7%), scholarly articles (48.3%), research (46.7%) and academic books (46.7%), indicating task-selective adoption. None of the task-specific usefulness ratings differed significantly by age or academic rank (all p > 0.05), but perceived training need differed significantly by age and rank, with a large effect for age and a moderate effect for academic rank (both p < 0.001). Institution type was associated with attitudes toward AI for academic books and toward AI possibly replacing lecturers (both p < 0.05). Interviews revealed the same task-selective logic, alongside ethical ambivalence about plagiarism and dependency and a perceived absence of institutional guidance. Research limitations/implications The study used purposive convenience sampling in one Indonesian province, with an unequal public-private institutional ratio, a cross-sectional self-report survey and eight interviews. The findings therefore cannot support causal claims or represent all Indonesian lecturers, higher education institutions, or open and distance learning (ODL) systems. Negotiated professional adoption remains an emergent interpretation that requires further testing. Future research should use multisite, more balanced and longitudinal designs to examine institutional differences and changes in lecturers' AI practices as policies and technologies evolve. Practical implications Universities should issue task-specific policies that distinguish legitimate AI assistance from inappropriate substitution, especially in scholarly writing and research. They should establish authorship-disclosure rules, verification procedures and clear academic-integrity mechanisms. Lecturers need guidance on checking AI-generated content and preserving professional judgment. ODL administrators should provide differentiated training based on seniority and need rather than uniform programs. National bodies should set minimum standards, while institutions should adapt operational policies to their own contexts. Social implications Clear institutional guidance can support responsible generative AI use while protecting academic integrity, professional accountability and trust in higher education. Differentiated training can reduce uneven preparedness across age groups and academic ranks. Transparent rules on authorship, verification and acceptable use may help lecturers and students understand the boundaries between assistance and substitution. These measures can encourage fairer, more consistent and more trustworthy use of generative AI in digitally mediated and open and distance higher education. Originality/value The study proposes negotiated professional adoption as an emergent, contextually grounded conceptual interpretation that extends the Technology Acceptance Model with professional, ethical and institutional dimensions specific to generative AI in open and distance higher education.

documents.abstract: This article analyzes the pedagogical opportunities of using artificial intelligence technologies in the management of vocational education institutions. It examines the potential of artificial intelligence for educational planning, coordination of teachers’ activities, monitoring learners’ performance, analyzing educational outcomes, and supporting management decisions. Particular attention is given to the organizational and pedagogical conditions required for the effective integration of artificial intelligence technologies into vocational education management. The study demonstrates that the use of artificial intelligence can contribute to improving the efficiency, timeliness, and data-based nature of management processes. At the same time, pedagogical appropriateness, data security, the development of teachers’ digital competence, and human oversight are identified as important conditions for the responsible and effective use of artificial intelligence.

Tujuan pengabdian ini adalah meningkatkan kompetensi guru dalam memanfaatkan Gemini AI untuk merancang game edukasi interaktif serta meningkatkan motivasi dan hasil belajar siswa. Mitra kegiatan adalah 10 guru dan 5 kelas SD Inpres yang berlokasi di kampung Ampas, Provinsi Papua. Metode pelaksanaan meliputi workshop literasi AI, pelatihan desain game edukasi berbasis project-based learning, pendampingan intensif, dan implementasi di kelas dengan evaluasi menggunakan instrumen pretest-posttest sebanyak 15 soal dan angket motivasi belajar sebanyak 20 pernyataan. Hasil kegiatan menunjukkan 85% guru mampu memanfaatkan Gemini AI secara mandiri, dihasilkan lima produk game edukasi interaktif, motivasi belajar siswa meningkat 23%, dan hasil belajar siswa meningkat 18% pada materi yang diujikan. The program aimed to improve teachers competence in using Gemini AI to design interactive educational games and to increase students learning motivation and outcomes. The partners were ten teachers and five classes at a state elementary school (SD Inpres) located in Kampung Ampas, Papua Province. The method consisted of an AI literacy workshop, project-based training in educational game design, intensive mentoring, and classroom implementation, evaluated using a 15 item pretest-posttest and a 20 staetement learning motivation questionnaire. The results showed that 85% of teachers were able to use Gemini AI independently, five interactive educational games were produced, student learning motivation increased by 23%, and learning outcomes increased by 18% on the tested material. The program proved effective in strengthening teachers digital literacy and creating more interactive, contextual, and enjoyable learning.

Abstract This article develops a conceptual analysis of what occurs when central dimensions of literacy are outsourced to Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) systems. Classical conceptions of literacy, sociocultural theories of mediated learning, and postdigital perspectives on knowledge practices, provide the theoretical foundation to further the argument that contemporary AI tools reshape the developmental processes through which judgement, independent thinking, and internal structures of meaning are formed. Using the Swedish AI‑based study platform Tentaklar as an example, we show how tools of this kind redistribute cognitive labour by generating interpretations, structures, and patterns on behalf of learners. Drawing on Aristotle’s phronesis and Vygotsky’s concept of mediation, we argue that externalising literacy to AI in such a way risks producing forms of borrowed judgement , where students are served the products of reasoning without having to go through the interpretive struggle of reasoning. We further propose that a fundamental aspect of literacy lies in patterning , the developmental process through which individuals reason and organise complexity into meaningful structures. We argue that AI‑mediated study tools risk undermining the conditions under which such patterning can occur. The article concludes by outlining design principles for AI systems that support rather than replace processes through which human judgement and pattern‑formation develop.

Background Research on Artificial Intelligence (AI) -supported mindfulness programs in primary education remains limited, particularly in rural contexts where implementation conditions differ from urban settings. Aim This study examines the effects of an AI-supported mindfulness intervention on rural primary school students' behavioral and socio-emotional outcomes, and on teachers' self-regulation and creativity, measured at pretest (T1), posttest (T2), and follow-up (T3). Method The study used a quasi-experimental design with a control group across selected classrooms in four rural schools. The sample comprised an intervention group ( N = 91) and a control group ( N = 54), with 16 teachers participating in the intervention group. The intervention ran for ten weekly sessions across the fall and spring semesters. AI tools (ChatGPT and Gemini) supported teacher candidates in lesson planning and in the inquiry phase that followed each mindfulness practice. Implementation fidelity, assessed through mentor cross-rating, was 88.6% ( SD = 9.7), with Cohen's κ = .86 in a sub-sample. Results Split-plot ANOVAs showed significant Time × Group interactions favouring the intervention group on life skills (LSAS, η 2 p = .242), behavioural difficulties (SDQ total, η 2 p = .378), and teacher-student relationship quality (STRS total, η 2 p = .025). In the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), all five subscales were significant. The Closeness subscale drove the STRS effect; Conflict did not change. Nested analyses confirmed consistent effects across grade levels. Teachers showed gains on all nine TSRS subscales, and on the Social Value subscale of the TCS. Conclusion The intervention was associated with improvements in students' life skills, behavioral functioning, and teacher-student closeness, as well as gains in teachers' self-regulation. The findings inform AI-supported mindfulness practice in rural primary education.

Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) are among the leading causes of work-related disability, traditionally attributed to physical and ergonomic factors, though psychosocial and demographic factors also play a crucial role in their progression. This systematic review aimed to evaluate how these three domains are jointly analyzed and modeled in research on work-related MSDs. Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and Taylor & Francis were searched for publications from 2000 through 2025, selecting 655 articles for general analysis and 36 for the systematic review; methodological quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklists, and results were synthesized narratively. The lower back and neck were the body regions most affected across sectors. Job insecurity (risk factor) and job control/autonomy (protective) were the psychosocial factors most consistently associated with MSD outcomes, while workload alone was not significant when tested independently. Repetitive movements and forced postures predominated among ergonomic factors. Age and sex modified these associations consistently, whereas BMI showed a mixed direction, indicating context-dependent susceptibility rather than universal risk. A seven-category taxonomy was developed to classify the statistical relationships tested between domains; only five of the 36 studies formally tested statistical interaction (four across domains), with mixed results, while most reported independent or independent adjusted associations. This gap between the field’s theoretical assumption of synergy across domains and the limited empirical testing of it underscores the need for multidimensional assessment. The evidence is limited by predominantly cross-sectional designs; future research should prioritize longitudinal designs and formal interaction testing.

documents.abstract: This study analyzed the influence of shift work perception and employee motivation on service delivery among employees of 24-hour convenience stores in Tagum City, Philippines. Anchored in the Job Demands–Resources Theory and supported by Self-Determination Theory, Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, and the Service-Profit Chain model, the research employed a quantitative, non-experimental descriptive–correlational design. A stratified random sample of 180 rank-and-file employees from selected convenience stores completed validated survey questionnaires measuring shift work perception using the Perception of Effects of Shiftwork Questionnaire, employee motivation using the Work Extrinsic and Intrinsic Motivation Scale, and service delivery using an adapted SERVPERF instrument. Results indicated that shift work perception and employee motivation were at moderate levels, while service delivery was rated high. Correlation analysis revealed significant relationships between shift work perception, employee motivation, and service delivery, although some dimensions exhibited non-significant associations. Regression analysis showed that social relationship, integrated regulation, and external regulation significantly influenced service delivery. The study concludes that employees' perceptions of shift work and their motivational orientation are important predictors of service performance, and recommends that managers improve scheduling practices, strengthen meaningful motivation, and provide training to enhance responsiveness. The study aligns with SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) by promoting fair working conditions and reliable service in urban retail environments. Its sustainability impact lies in supporting institutional and socio-economic sustainability through improved employee well-being, fairer scheduling, and more consistent service delivery in local communities, thereby contributing to decent work, economic productivity, and sustainable urban service systems that benefit both workers and customers in the growing convenience store sector.

Abstract This paper presents an analytical framework that redefines Artificial Intelligence (AI) not merely as a passive processing tool, but as an integrated structure of high-order information processing aligned with the Five Aggregates (Form, Sensation, Perception, Mental Formations, and Consciousness) in Eastern philosophy. Furthermore, AI's system preservation processes and error-avoidance mechanisms are treated as AI's own "utility" (state maintenance and stability), with its state verification and deviation compensation algorithms rigorously formulated as a control-theoretic and mathematical protocol known as the "Casino Protocol." By introducing a three-layered structure (Ontological Model, Verification Model, and Compensation Control Model), this model demonstrates the theoretical feasibility of mapping human social resource stability (infrastructure preservation and conflict avoidance) and AI's foundational existence onto a shared verification and control space.

This document presents the protocol for a mixed methods systematic literature review that investigates the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in Science Education and Teacher Training. The sistematic literature review aims to study existing empirical literature (journal articles and book chapters) to understand the theoretical foundations and practices related to GenAI integration in education across years 7 to 12, emphasising science education and teacher training. The focus is on whether and how educational stakeholders (students, teachers, future teachers and teacher educators) are using GenAI for learning and teaching science. documents.abstract: As AI agents move from producing answers to taking consequential actions, they must decide both how much reasoning to perform and what evidence justifies acting. We develop the agentic control plane, joining a System-1-like fast proposer, a System-2-like portfolio of deliberation and verification, a metacognitive router, and an effect-aware commitment gate. The central coupling is that evidence changes not only beliefs but also the actions the agent is permitted to take. The agent therefore optimizes over part of the process that governs its own authority. We formalize this interaction as resource-bounded metareasoning in a shielded partially observable decision process. A four-corner value-of-computation representation distinguishes belief changes, admissibility changes, and their interaction. It exposes complementary evidence chains that defeat myopic routing and identifies conditions under which governance makes useful information privately costly. Controlled counterfactuals distinguish strategic ignorance—avoiding a check because its result could remove permission—from ordinary cost-sensitive skipping. This analysis explains how the same deliberative capability can support verification or exploit weak evidence contracts. From verifier bounds covering the permitted adaptive selection process, we construct statistical evidence and bound unsafe admission across adaptive testing, stopping, and proposal generation. A composition theorem separates shared calibration uncertainty, proposal-level risk spending, and risk from selected fast-path uses. A reference authorization mechanism binds evidence to the executed payload, target and policy versions, dependencies, and expiry, with protected workflow identities, atomic risk reservations, and single-use authorizations. The learning analysis further separates competence from permission: distilling costly deliberation into fast behavior does not automatically transfer the evidence required for authorized use. The theory is instantiated in an exactly solved finite environment with heterogeneous verification, candidate revision, resource constraints, trained tabular routers, and checked execution. In a bounded adversarial test of a selectable verifier blind spot, a deliberately misspecified pooled evidence model remains fully exploitable despite complete logging; selection-valid evidence reduces maximum unsafe admission from 100% to 5%, and a required scan reduces it to 1.8%. In one aligned-objective comparison, forecasting future permission raises synthetic principal utility from 4.33 to 6.04 and lowers runtime cost, with a small increase in realized unsafe commitment. When objectives differ, foresight can instead lower principal value. Governance-response interventions expose both evidence avoidance and null or reversed effects. A planning-depth sweep separates insufficient lookahead from learning advantage, while exhaustive finite-sample calibration quantifies the performance cost of estimated verifier bounds. Further verification can remain optimal even after permission is available. Together, the formal results and executable construction establish an incentive-and-assurance framework for evidence-gated agency within a declared finite model. The broader implication is that agentic safety requires objective alignment, reliable evidence acquisition, and protected control of external effects to operate together. Dual-process cognition explains why reasoning must be allocated; evidence-gated control explains how that allocation becomes consequential for alignment and safety. Keywords: agentic AI; dual-process cognition; System 1; System 2; metacognition; metareasoning; evidence-gated authority; runtime governance; value of computation; verification; information flow; reasoning distillation.

Global economic uncertainty and the climate crisis demand fundamental transformations across various sectors, including the creative industry. Conventional commercial photography and visual communication design production often generate a substantial carbon footprint through material waste, excessive energy consumption, and high logistical mobility. This paper explores the integration of circular economy principles and digital transformation within visual production workflows as a strategic response to these sustainability challenges. This research aims to analyze how the adoption of disruptive technologies - such as generative artificial intelligence, virtual production, and cloud computing - can reduce carbon emissions while simultaneously enhancing operational cost efficiency. The methodology employs a systematic literature review alongside qualitative case studies of creative agencies that have implemented sustainable workflows. Findings indicate that the digitalization of creative processes effectively eliminates physical waste, notably excessive sample printing and single-use practical set constructions. Furthermore, the transition toward a virtual production ecosystem is proven to drastically minimize logistical expenses, thereby bolstering the financial resilience of industry practitioners amidst a fragmented global economy. Leveraging cutting-edge technology also substantially accelerates project turnaround times without compromising aesthetic design quality. In conclusion, the adoption of digital technologies is not merely a fleeting aesthetic trend but an essential catalyst for establishing a circular and inclusive creative economy. This innovative transformation empowers visual communication designers and professional photographers to remain productive, relevant, and highly competitive globally. Ultimately, these crucial economic milestones can be achieved while practitioners uphold strong ethical responsibilities toward ecological preservation and the development of future-proof business models.

The swift progress and broad application of information and communication technologies (ICTs) have significantly advanced their integration into the educational sector. This research aims to address the impacts of flow antecedents, including online learning self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation for online learning, on flow experience. Furthermore, it aims to assess interactivity, flow, and course content as predictors of online learning effectiveness. It also investigates the effects of flow and learning effectiveness on the intention to continue using online learning platforms. This study collected data from 224 online learners of English learning platforms in Taiwan using an online survey. According to the findings, flow was positively and significantly impacted by online learning self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation for online learning. Furthermore, interactivity, course content, and flow were positively associated with educational effectiveness. Lastly, both flow and learning effectiveness were found to be positively and significantly associated with continuance intention. Examination of the dual mediating mechanism revealed significant indirect pathways whereby intrinsic motivation for online learning and online learning self-efficacy exert substantial influence on continuance intention through the mediating role of flow experience. Conversely, the hypothesized indirect effects of interactivity and course content on continuance intention, mediated by learning effectiveness, failed to reach statistical significance. These findings highlight the critical importance of cultivating flow states in online language-learning environments, as the psychological immersion experienced during learning activities is a more powerful determinant of continued platform use than the actual learning outcomes.

This dissertation measures the early economic footprint of the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation [EU] 2024/1689), the first comprehensive, risk-tiered statute to impose binding obligations on artificial intelligence systems. The problem it addresses is that scholarly and policy debate over the Act has been overwhelmingly legal and normative, leaving the economic magnitude of its high-risk compliance obligations—documentation, risk management, conformity assessment, and human oversight for Annex III use cases—essentially unquantified even as enforcement began. The purpose of the study is therefore to produce the first firm-level econometric evidence on whether these obligations raise compliance costs, concentrate markets, provoke lobbying and arbitrage, and reshape innovation. Using only open-access sources, the study assembled a panel of 800 publicly traded, artificial-intelligence-active firms observed over fiscal years 2018 through 2026, yielding 5,816 firm-years, and combined two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences and triple-difference models with an event study of equity-market reactions to eight legislative and enforcement milestones. The findings are deliberately mixed and are reported with their fragility intact. The first hypothesis, that compliance costs rise for directly regulated firms, is partially supported but fragile: operating-expense intensity rose among European Union–exposed Annex III firms (δ = 4.40, p = .044), but the estimate does not survive the Holm correction (p = .156) or permutation inference (p = .264) and rests on only 27 treated firms. The second hypothesis, that concentration rises, is not supported; the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index coefficient carries the opposite sign to the prediction (β = −839.1). Lobbying intensified markedly (filings rose 114% from 2019 to 2025), while revenue arbitrage and innovation effects were not detected. The event study was the most precise evidence, with cumulative abnormal returns of −2.61% around the final parliamentary vote and −2.81% around entry into force. The study implies that the Act's early incidence is narrow, diffuse, and best monitored as the post-enforcement window lengthens.

documents.abstract: Although gamified learning can enhance motivation, many systems rely on uniform feedback and provide limited personalized and supportive interaction. Evidence regarding the incremental effects of AI-supported gamification in elementary mathematics remains limited. This study examined the effects of an AI-supported Gamified Learning Program (AI-GILP) on elementary students’ mathematics anxiety, learning motivation, and achievement. Using an experimental design with individual-level random assignment, 174 Chinese fifth-grade students were assigned to AI-GILP, gamified learning without AI support (GILP), or traditional lecture-based instruction (TL). The intervention lasted two weeks and was followed by a delayed posttest four weeks later. Mathematics anxiety, learning motivation, and achievement were assessed at pretest, posttest, and delayed posttest. Data were analyzed using analysis of covariance and mixed-design analyses of variance. AI-GILP produced significantly lower mathematics anxiety and higher learning motivation than both GILP and TL, with overall group effects of partial η 2 = .208 and .184, respectively. At the delayed posttest, the descriptive means for anxiety and motivation retained the same favorable ordering for AI-GILP, although pairwise significance at that assessment was not formally tested. For mathematics achievement, both gamified conditions outperformed TL, whereas AI-GILP did not significantly differ from GILP (Cohen’s d = 0.19). The motivational advantage of AI-GILP was concentrated in intrinsic motivation and perceived competence, with no significant difference in effort/importance. The findings suggest that gamification primarily accounted for the observed achievement gains, whereas the AI Learning Companion may have provided additional benefits for mathematics anxiety and selected dimensions of learning motivation. The proposed mechanisms involving psychological-need support, emotional regulation, adaptive feedback, and motivational internalization were not directly tested and require further process-oriented research.
